name: Network Routing
description: Network routing involves determining optimal paths for data packets to travel from source to destination nodes across a dynamic graph of routers and links. The problem requires balancing multiple objectives including minimizing latency, maximizing throughput, avoiding congestion, and maintaining reliability under node and link failures. Routing must adapt continuously to changing network topology and traffic conditions without centralized coordination in large-scale networks. Distributed routing protocols must converge on loop-free paths quickly after topology changes while scaling to millions of nodes.
key_challenges: Dynamic topology changes from node and link failures
Multi-objective optimization across latency, throughput, and reliability
Convergence speed after topology changes
Scalability to internet-scale networks with millions of nodes
Handling asymmetric link capacities and heterogeneous traffic demands
Avoiding routing loops during convergence

mathematical_properties.graph_theoretic: Shortest path on weighted directed graphs; generalizes to multi-commodity flow
mathematical_properties.solution_space: Exponential in number of paths; polynomial for single-objective with Dijkstra
mathematical_properties.objective: Minimize cost function over path selection variables subject to capacity constraints

state_of_art_baseline: OSPF/IS-IS for intra-domain; BGP for inter-domain; ECMP for load balancing

name: Traveling Salesman Problem
description: The Traveling Salesman Problem requires finding the shortest Hamiltonian cycle visiting all nodes in a weighted graph exactly once and returning to the origin. Despite its simple formulation, TSP is NP-hard and serves as a canonical benchmark for combinatorial optimization algorithms. Practical variants include asymmetric TSP with directed edge costs, time-windowed TSP with delivery constraints, and multi-depot vehicle routing extensions. Real-world applications span logistics, circuit board drilling, DNA sequencing, and telescope scheduling. The problem's difficulty stems from the super-exponential growth of the solution space combined with the absence of useful convex structure.
key_challenges: Super-exponential solution space of n! permutations
No polynomial-time exact algorithm known
Highly multimodal objective landscape with many local optima
Scaling to instances with tens of thousands of cities
Maintaining solution quality under time constraints
Extending to practical variants with additional constraints

mathematical_properties.problem_class: NP-hard; in APX for metric instances
mathematical_properties.graph_theoretic: Minimum weight Hamiltonian cycle on complete weighted graph
mathematical_properties.solution_space: n!/2 distinct tours for symmetric TSP
mathematical_properties.objective: Minimize sum of edge weights in Hamiltonian cycle

state_of_art_baseline: Concorde exact solver; LKH3 heuristic achieving within 0.1% of optimal on most benchmarks

name: Job Scheduling
description: Job scheduling problems involve assigning a set of tasks with resource requirements, precedence constraints, and deadlines to a set of machines or processors to optimize objectives such as makespan, total weighted completion time, or number of tardy jobs. The problem encompasses a family of variants from single-machine scheduling with known polynomial solutions to parallel machine and job shop scheduling problems that are NP-hard. Modern data center scheduling must handle thousands of concurrent jobs with heterogeneous resource demands across GPU, CPU, memory, and network dimensions. Dynamic online scheduling requires real-time decisions without foreknowledge of future job arrivals.
key_challenges: NP-hardness of general multi-machine variants
Handling precedence constraints and resource dependencies
Online scheduling without future job arrival knowledge
Multi-dimensional resource packing across heterogeneous job types
Balancing fairness with efficiency objectives
Adapting to job failures and rescheduling requirements

mathematical_properties.problem_class: NP-hard for most multi-machine variants; P for some single-machine variants
mathematical_properties.graph_theoretic: Precedence constraints form DAG; scheduling maps to graph coloring and topological ordering
mathematical_properties.objective: Minimize makespan or weighted sum of completion times subject to precedence and resource constraints

benchmark_suite: JSSP benchmarks by Fisher and Thompson
state_of_art_baseline: List scheduling heuristics; branch and bound for small instances; FIFO and SJF for online variants

name: Distributed Consensus
description: Distributed consensus requires a set of nodes in a network to agree on a single value despite the possibility of node failures, message delays, and network partitions. The problem is foundational to distributed databases, blockchain systems, and fault-tolerant computing. The CAP theorem establishes fundamental trade-offs between consistency, availability, and partition tolerance that any consensus protocol must navigate. Byzantine consensus, where up to a fraction of nodes may behave arbitrarily maliciously, imposes stricter requirements on protocol design and requires at least 3f+1 nodes to tolerate f Byzantine failures. Practical systems must achieve consensus within bounded latency under realistic network conditions.
key_challenges: FLP impossibility: no deterministic protocol guarantees termination in asynchronous networks
Byzantine fault tolerance requires 3f+1 nodes for f faulty nodes
CAP theorem trade-offs between consistency and availability under partitions
Leader election and view change under high message loss
Scaling consensus throughput to thousands of nodes
Preventing livelock and ensuring progress under adversarial timing

mathematical_properties.problem_class: Computationally solvable with randomization; impossible deterministically in fully asynchronous model
mathematical_properties.graph_theoretic: Requires network connectivity above fault tolerance threshold
mathematical_properties.solution_space: Protocol state space exponential in number of nodes
mathematical_properties.objective: Guarantee safety (agreement, validity) and liveness (termination) properties

state_of_art_baseline: Raft for crash fault tolerance; PBFT and Tendermint for Byzantine tolerance; HotStuff for leader-based BFT

name: Continuous Function Optimization
description: Continuous function optimization involves finding the global minimum or maximum of a real-valued objective function over a continuous search space, typically in high dimensions. The problem encompasses both black-box optimization where only function evaluations are available and white-box optimization where gradient information is accessible. Many real-world engineering design, hyperparameter tuning, and scientific calibration problems reduce to continuous optimization with expensive-to-evaluate objectives. Multimodal functions with many local optima require global search strategies that balance exploration of the search space with exploitation of promising regions.
key_challenges: Curse of dimensionality: search space volume grows exponentially with dimensions
Multimodal functions with exponentially many local optima
Expensive function evaluations limiting number of feasible iterations
Noisy function evaluations requiring robust estimation
Unknown gradient information in black-box settings
Balancing exploration and exploitation in limited evaluation budget

mathematical_properties.problem_class: NP-hard for general non-convex functions; P for convex functions
mathematical_properties.topological: Solution landscape characterized by Morse theory; difficulty scales with number of saddle points
mathematical_properties.objective: Find x* = argmin f(x) for potentially non-convex f: R^n to R

state_of_art_baseline: CMA-ES for medium dimensions; L-BFGS-B for gradient-available cases; Bayesian optimization for expensive evaluations

name: Data Clustering
description: Data clustering partitions a dataset into groups such that intra-cluster similarity is maximized and inter-cluster similarity is minimized, without using predefined class labels. The problem is fundamental to unsupervised learning with applications in customer segmentation, document organization, anomaly detection, and bioinformatics. Cluster structure can take arbitrary shapes including convex blobs, rings, filaments, and hierarchical nested structures, requiring algorithms to adapt to unknown geometry. The number of clusters is typically unknown a priori and must be inferred from the data. Scalability to high-dimensional datasets with millions of points presents additional challenges.
key_challenges: Unknown number of clusters requiring automatic determination
Arbitrary cluster shapes violating convexity assumptions of k-means
High-dimensional data suffering from curse of dimensionality in distance metrics
Scalability to millions of data points
Sensitivity to initialization and local minima
Defining appropriate similarity metrics for mixed data types

mathematical_properties.problem_class: NP-hard for k-means with k >= 2; heuristic solutions dominate practice
mathematical_properties.information_theoretic: Related to mutual information maximization between cluster assignments and data
mathematical_properties.solution_space: Exponential in number of possible partitions: Bell number B(n)
mathematical_properties.objective: Minimize within-cluster variance or maximize between-cluster separation under chosen metric

state_of_art_baseline: k-means++ for spherical clusters; DBSCAN for arbitrary shapes; Gaussian Mixture Models for probabilistic clustering

name: Resource Allocation
description: Resource allocation problems involve distributing limited resources among competing agents or tasks to optimize system-wide objectives such as total utility, fairness, or efficiency. The problem arises in cloud computing, wireless spectrum assignment, supply chain management, and financial portfolio optimization. Multi-agent resource allocation must often satisfy individual rationality and incentive compatibility constraints when agents have private utility information. Dynamic variants require real-time reallocation as resource availability and demand fluctuate. The combination of integer constraints, multiple objectives, and strategic agent behavior makes general resource allocation computationally intractable.
key_challenges: Integer constraints making exact optimization NP-hard for combinatorial variants
Multiple competing objectives including efficiency, fairness, and revenue
Strategic agents with private utility information requiring mechanism design
Dynamic demand and supply requiring real-time adaptive allocation
Scalability to thousands of resources and agents
Ensuring envy-freeness and proportionality in fair division variants

mathematical_properties.problem_class: NP-hard for combinatorial auction variants; polynomial relaxations often used
mathematical_properties.game_theoretic: Nash equilibrium existence guaranteed in compact convex strategy spaces
mathematical_properties.solution_space: Combinatorial allocation space exponential in resources times agents
mathematical_properties.objective: Maximize social welfare or Nash social welfare subject to resource capacity and feasibility constraints

existing_bio_inspired: Particle Swarm for cloud resource scheduling
state_of_art_baseline: Linear programming relaxation with branch and bound; greedy approximation algorithms with provable guarantees; auction mechanisms for strategic settings
